chunks: From him (Al-Shaykh), from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
That he (peace be upon him) disliked for a man to stay with his debtor. He said: 'He should not eat from his food, nor drink from his drink, nor eat fodder from his fodder.'

key_terms.كَرِهَ: Disliked (makruh, a recommended but not obligatory ruling)
key_terms.يَعْتَلِفُ: To eat fodder (used for animals, implying taking animal feed)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a creditor staying with their debtor in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam Al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) ruled that it is disliked (makruh) for a creditor to stay with their debtor to ensure repayment, specifically prohibiting the consumption of the debtor's food, drink, or fodder. This ruling highlights the Shia emphasis on preserving the debtor's dignity and preventing the creditor from imposing an undue financial burden beyond the principal debt. It reflects the broader jurisprudential principle of *israf* (extravagance or excessive burden) in debt collection, ensuring the relationship remains equitable rather than exploitative.
